subject: Geography
name: Geography, Levels 7 and 8
syllabus: Victorian Curriculum F-10 Version 2.0: Geography, Levels 7 and 8

points.title: Renewable and non-renewable resources
points.brief: A renewable resource is replaced by natural processes, while a non-renewable one runs out once used. Water is renewable because the water cycle keeps replacing it, though some stores refill very slowly.

points.title: The water cycle
points.brief: Water moves between the oceans, air and land through evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, runoff and infiltration, changing between liquid, gas and ice.

points.title: Where the Earth's water is stored
points.brief: Almost all water is salty and in the oceans. Most fresh water is locked in ice or held underground in aquifers, and only a tiny share is in rivers and lakes.

points.title: How flows of water connect places
points.brief: Rivers and groundwater carry water, sediment, nutrients and pollution from one place to another, so what happens upstream changes places downstream, as in the Murray-Darling Basin.

points.title: Ways people use and value water
points.brief: Water has environmental value for ecosystems, economic value for farms, industry and power, and cultural, spiritual and aesthetic value, such as places of meaning or beauty.

points.title: Water and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples
points.brief: For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples, rivers, waterholes, springs and seas are part of Country, with cultural and spiritual meaning, and knowledge of finding and caring for water is passed down through generations.

points.title: Water in the Asia region
points.brief: Water shapes life in Asia, such as monsoon rains for rice farming, the Mekong River's fisheries and the sacred meaning of the Ganges in Hinduism.

points.title: Australia's rainfall and water resources
points.brief: Australia is the driest inhabited continent. Most rain falls on the northern and eastern coasts and in Tasmania, while much of the inland is arid, so water is unevenly spread.

points.title: Variable rainfall in Australia
points.brief: Australia's rainfall changes a lot from year to year, linked to El Niño (often drier) and La Niña (often wetter), which is why droughts and floods are common and dams store water.

points.title: Climate change and Australia's water
points.brief: Forecasts show less cool-season rain in southern Australia, more evaporation as it warms and heavier downpours, which puts pressure on water supplies.

points.title: Physical and economic water scarcity
points.brief: Physical scarcity means there is not enough water to meet demand, often from low rainfall or overuse. Economic scarcity means water exists but people lack the money or infrastructure to reach it.

points.title: Managing water scarcity in Australia
points.brief: Australia overcomes scarcity with dams, desalination plants, recycled water, water restrictions, efficient irrigation, rainwater tanks and water trading between users in the Murray-Darling Basin.

points.title: Water scarcity in West Asia and North Africa
points.brief: This is the most water-scarce region. Countries rely on desalination, ancient groundwater and shared rivers such as the Nile and the Tigris and Euphrates, which can cause tension between nations.

points.title: Natural hazards and disasters
points.brief: A natural hazard is an event that could harm people or property. It becomes a disaster when it causes major damage or loss of life that a community cannot cope with on its own.

points.title: Tropical cyclones
points.brief: Cyclones form over warm tropical oceans and bring destructive winds, heavy rain and storm surges, mostly to northern Australia between November and April.

points.title: Floods
points.brief: Floods happen when heavy rain makes rivers overflow or water pool faster than it drains. Flash floods rise in hours; river floods build over days across wide plains.

points.title: Drought
points.brief: A drought is a long period of below-average rainfall. It dries up water supplies, ruins crops and pasture, and hurts farm incomes and rural towns.

points.title: Bushfires
points.brief: Hot, dry, windy weather and dry fuel make bushfire risk high. Fires threaten lives, homes and ecosystems, especially in south-eastern Australia in summer.

points.title: Preparing for and responding to hazards
points.brief: Communities reduce harm through forecasting, warnings, building rules, levees and fire plans before a hazard, then emergency response and recovery after it.

points.title: What liveability means
points.brief: Liveability is how well a place supports a good quality of life for the people who live there, such as safety, health, jobs, services and a pleasant environment.

points.title: Measures of liveability
points.brief: Liveability rankings score places on environmental, economic and social measures, such as crime, health care, education, transport, housing costs and pollution.

points.title: Liveability and where people live
points.brief: People are drawn to places they see as liveable, but what counts as liveable differs with age, income, culture and needs, such as a family wanting schools or a retiree wanting quiet.

points.title: Judging liveability with geographical concepts
points.brief: Geographers judge liveability using space (where services are), environment (the quality of surroundings) and interconnection (links to people, jobs and other places).

points.title: Access to services and facilities
points.brief: How close and easy it is to reach schools, hospitals, shops and transport shapes how liveable a place feels. Remote places often have fewer services and rely on telehealth and online learning.

points.title: Environmental quality and liveability
points.brief: Clean air and water, green space, low noise and attractive surroundings make people see a place as more liveable.

points.title: Social connectedness and community identity
points.brief: Feeling safe, belonging to a community, and having friends, family, clubs and shared events nearby all raise how liveable people find a place.

points.title: Connection to Country and Place
points.brief: For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples, Country includes land, waters, sky and kin. Being connected to Country and Place supports identity, culture and wellbeing, and shapes how liveable a place is.

points.title: Improving liveability locally
points.brief: Councils and communities make places more liveable with parks, bike paths, community centres, better public transport, street trees and safer streets.

points.title: Landscapes and landforms
points.brief: A landform is a single natural feature of the Earth's surface, such as a hill or valley. A landscape is a larger area made of many landforms together.

points.title: Types of landscapes
points.brief: Landscapes include mountain, coastal, riverine, desert, karst (limestone) and volcanic landscapes, each with its own typical landforms.

points.title: Australia's major landforms
points.brief: Australia is old, low and flat, with the Great Dividing Range in the east, the Central Lowlands, and the Western Plateau covering most of the west.

points.title: Why people value landscapes
points.brief: People value landscapes for their beauty, for recreation and tourism, for the resources they hold, and for their spiritual and cultural meaning.

points.title: Landscapes in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures
points.brief: Landforms carry deep cultural and spiritual meaning for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples, such as Uluru for the Anangu and Gariwerd (the Grampians) for the Djab Wurrung and Jardwadjali peoples.

points.title: Weathering
points.brief: Weathering breaks rock down where it sits, through physical processes like frost and heat, chemical processes like rain dissolving limestone, and living things like roots.

points.title: Erosion, transport and deposition
points.brief: Erosion wears away and removes rock and soil by water, wind or ice. The material is carried away and dropped somewhere else, which builds new landforms.

points.title: River landforms
points.brief: Rivers cut V-shaped valleys and waterfalls near their source, form meanders and oxbow lakes in their middle course, and build floodplains and deltas where they slow down.

points.title: Coastal landforms
points.brief: Waves erode headlands into cliffs, caves, arches and stacks, such as the Twelve Apostles, and deposit sand to form beaches, spits and dunes.

points.title: Tectonic forces and landforms
points.brief: Moving tectonic plates fold and fault rock to build mountains and rift valleys, and push up volcanoes where magma reaches the surface.

points.title: Human causes of landform change
points.brief: Mining, quarrying, building, dams, land clearing and farming change landforms directly or speed up erosion.

points.title: Managing coasts
points.brief: Hard engineering such as sea walls and groynes protects coasts but can move erosion elsewhere. Soft approaches such as beach nourishment and replanting dunes work with natural processes.

points.title: Protecting landscapes
points.brief: National parks, World Heritage listing and rules on development protect landforms, and Traditional Owners often share in managing them.

points.title: Explaining landforms with interconnection and change
points.brief: Interconnection shows how processes such as climate, rivers and people link to shape a landform. Change shows how it formed over long time spans and can be altered quickly.

points.title: What a geomorphological hazard is
points.brief: A hazard caused by processes in or on the Earth's crust, such as earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, tsunamis and landslides, most common along plate boundaries.

points.title: Earthquakes
points.brief: Earthquakes happen when rock along a fault slips suddenly. Their impacts include collapsed buildings, landslides and fires, and they are worst where buildings are weak and populations dense.

points.title: Volcanic eruptions
points.brief: Volcanoes form where magma rises, often at plate boundaries such as the Pacific Ring of Fire. Eruptions bring lava, ash, gas and mudflows, but volcanic soils are also fertile.

points.title: Tsunamis
points.brief: A tsunami is a series of huge waves, usually set off by an undersea earthquake. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami showed how far the damage can spread.

points.title: Reducing the risk of geomorphological hazards
points.brief: Communities cut the harm with warning systems, earthquake-resistant buildings, land-use planning, evacuation drills and aid after the event.

points.title: Urbanisation and why it happens
points.brief: Urbanisation is the growing share of people living in towns and cities. People are pushed from rural areas by poverty and few jobs, and pulled to cities by work, services and education.

points.title: Impacts of rapid urbanisation
points.brief: Fast city growth can bring jobs and higher incomes, but also slums, traffic, pollution, water shortages and the loss of farmland. Megacities of over 10 million people feel these pressures most.

points.title: Urbanisation in Indonesia
points.brief: Jakarta grew fast as people moved from rural areas for work. Flooding, traffic and the city sinking from groundwater pumping led Indonesia to build a new capital, Nusantara, on Borneo.

points.title: Urbanisation in China
points.brief: China moved from a mostly rural to a mostly urban country in a few decades, as factories drew workers to coastal cities, bringing growth but also pollution and crowding.

points.title: Internal and international migration
points.brief: Internal migration is moving within a country. International migration is moving between countries. Both are driven by push and pull factors.

points.title: Migration and Australia's cities
points.brief: Most migrants to Australia settle in the capital cities, especially Sydney and Melbourne, which is a large part of why those cities keep growing.

points.title: Internal migration in Australia
points.brief: Australians move between places too, such as to Queensland and Western Australia for work or climate, and from cities to the coast or country for a sea change or tree change.

points.title: Internal migration in China
points.brief: Hundreds of millions of rural Chinese have moved to cities for factory and service work, one of the largest migrations in history, shaped by the hukou household registration system.

points.title: Australia's urban pattern
points.brief: Australia is one of the most urbanised countries. Most people live in a few large capital cities near the coast, and each capital is far bigger than the next town in its state.

points.title: Comparing Australia and the United States
points.brief: Both countries are highly urbanised, but the United States has many large cities spread across the country, while Australia's people are packed into a handful of coastal capitals.

points.title: Urban sprawl
points.brief: Sprawl is a city spreading outward in low-density suburbs. It uses up farmland and bush, lengthens travel, and makes services and public transport harder to provide.

points.title: Making cities more sustainable
points.brief: Cities become more sustainable with better public transport, homes closer to jobs, energy-efficient buildings, recycling and protected green space.

points.title: Cities and climate change
points.brief: Cities trap heat in the urban heat island effect, which climate change makes worse. They adapt with street trees, cool roofs, shade and flood-safe planning.

points.title: Understanding urbanisation through geographical concepts
points.brief: Space, place, interconnection, change and sustainability help explain where cities grow, what they are like, how they link to rural areas and whether their growth can last.

points.title: Map scale and direction
points.brief: Scale shows how distance on a map relates to real distance, as a ratio, a line or words. Compass points and a north arrow give direction.

points.title: Grid references, latitude and longitude
points.brief: Area and grid references find places on a map by its grid squares, eastings then northings. Latitude and longitude locate any place on Earth in degrees north or south and east or west.

points.title: Contour lines on topographic maps
points.brief: Contour lines join points of the same height. Lines close together show steep slopes and lines far apart show gentle ones.

points.title: Geospatial technologies
points.brief: GPS, satellite images and geographic information systems (GIS) collect and layer information about places so patterns can be mapped and studied.

points.title: Climate graphs
points.brief: A climate graph shows a place's average monthly rainfall as columns and temperature as a line, so its seasons and climate can be read at a glance.

points.title: Geographical inquiry questions
points.brief: Good inquiry questions ask what and where something is, why it is there, how it affects people and places, and what should be done.

points.title: Primary and secondary data
points.brief: Primary data is collected first-hand, such as fieldwork surveys and measurements. Secondary data comes from others, such as census figures, reports and maps.

points.title: Patterns, trends and relationships
points.brief: A pattern is how something is spread across space, a trend is a change over time, and a relationship is how two things change together.

points.title: Drawing conclusions and choosing actions
points.brief: A sound conclusion rests on evidence and considers ethical values, such as fairness. A good action weighs its environmental, economic and social effects.
